title: Under a Centimeter: Surveillance, Growth, and the Decision to Operate
subtitle: A subcentimeter papillary microcarcinoma from second opinion to final pathology
description: Interpreting a normal thyroid panel, managing repeated indeterminate cytology, deciding when active surveillance has failed, preoperative nerve responsibilities, reading a BRAF-negative papillary carcinoma, and what happened to the central compartment nodes.

steps.title: Step 1/6: What the TSH Decides
steps.scenario:
A 41-year-old woman is referred for a second opinion. A routine health screen found a firm, palpable mass in the right lower central neck. She has no voice change, no dysphagia, no radiation history, and no family history of thyroid cancer.

She brings outside laboratory results, and you complete the panel yourself:

    TSH                     1.76 microIU/mL
    Free T4                 0.90 ng/dL
    Anti-TPO antibody       < 0.3 IU/mL
    Anti-thyroglobulin Ab   1.8 IU/mL
    Thyroglobulin           1.77 ng/mL

You scan her yourself. The right lobe contains a 0.66 x 0.60 x 0.61 cm nodule: solid, markedly hypoechoic, lobulated with an irregular boundary, an incomplete halo, no calcification, and hard on elastography. A right level III node measures 0.71 x 0.38 cm, oval, regular, with a preserved linear hilus.
steps.media: Load image: Right thyroid nodule, longitudinal and transverse grayscale, unannotated. Caption: 'Right lobe.'
steps.question: What does her TSH of 1.76 microIU/mL tell you?

options.text: (A) It excludes an autonomously functioning nodule and keeps her on the sonographic pathway; within the normal range it does not risk-stratify this nodule
(B) A TSH in the lower half of the normal range is itself reassuring, since malignancy risk rises with TSH
(C) It excludes underlying autoimmune thyroiditis, which characteristically raises TSH
(D) It is normal, so thyroid function needs no further attention during her management

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

TSH is the branch point of the workup and it does one specific job. A suppressed TSH would raise the possibility of an autonomously functioning nodule, which is very rarely malignant, and would send you to scintigraphy rather than to a needle. Hers is normal, so that branch closes cleanly and the nodule is assessed on its sonographic merits: solid, markedly hypoechoic, lobulated with an irregular boundary, and hard on elastography, in a mass she can feel.

Why the others fail:
(B) The association between higher TSH and thyroid malignancy is real in population studies, but the effect is small and it has never been used to risk-stratify an individual nodule. A TSH of 1.76 tells you which pathway she is on. It does not tell you how likely her nodule is to be cancer, and reading it as reassurance would be reading a population statistic as a personal one.
(C) Euthyroid autoimmune thyroiditis is common, and seronegative disease is well described. This patient turns out to be an example of both: her anti-TPO is below the detection limit and her TSH is normal, yet her final histology reports lymphocytic thyroiditis with fibrosis and calcification in the non-neoplastic gland. Normal function does not exclude the disease, and a negative antibody does not either.
(D) True today and false later. If she proceeds to a lobectomy, roughly a quarter to a third of patients become hypothyroid and need replacement, so the TSH changes from a diagnostic test into the monitoring test that decides whether she takes a tablet for the rest of her life.

The rest of the panel is a baseline rather than a diagnostic test, and that is the right way to read it. Thyroglobulin is not interpretable as a tumor marker while the gland is intact, since normal tissue produces it; its value arrives after surgery, and having a preoperative figure on file is useful when the postoperative numbers need context. The anti-thyroglobulin antibody matters for a related reason: antibody positivity interferes with thyroglobulin assays and makes the result uninterpretable, so a documented negative now means any future thyroglobulin can be trusted.

On the level III node: oval, regular boundary, preserved linear fatty hilus. That is a normal reactive node, and seeing a node is not the same as finding one.

Keypoint: the TSH decides which pathway she is on, and once it comes back normal the nodule is judged on the ultrasound and the examining finger.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. 2015 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.

steps.title: Step 2/6: The Needle
steps.scenario:
A palpable, firm, sonographically suspicious nodule in a woman referred specifically because of a lump in her neck. You aspirate it yourself, under your own ultrasound guidance.

The target is 6.6 mm, solid, with an irregular margin, sitting close to the anterior capsule of the right lobe. There is no cystic component.

A trainee sets up the trolley and asks what you want on it.
steps.media: Load video: Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of a small solid thyroid nodule, needle tip visualized within the lesion. 10 seconds, muted.
steps.question: What do you ask for, and how do you sample?

options.text: (A) A 25 to 27 gauge needle, minimal or no suction, with several seconds of needle undulation inside the lesion
(B) A 22 gauge needle with continuous strong suction, to maximise cellular yield from a small solid target
(C) An 18 gauge core needle, since a repeat aspirate after an indeterminate result is unlikely to add anything
(D) A 25 to 27 gauge needle, sampling the periphery of the lesion only, to reduce the risk of needle track seeding

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The commonest reason a thyroid aspirate comes back non-diagnostic is blood, not lack of technique. A fine needle with little or no suction bleeds less, and the cells are collected by the shearing action of moving the needle through the lesion rather than by pulling on the plunger. Standard practice is a 25 to 27 gauge needle on a 5 to 10 mL syringe, with roughly five seconds of undulation within the target. In a 6.6 mm lesion the thing that determines success is not the gauge at all but whether you can keep the tip visualized inside it, which is why this aspirate is done under your own ultrasound rather than free-hand.

Why the others fail:
(B) The intuition that a bigger bore and harder suction give more cells is exactly backwards. Both increase hemorrhage, and blood dilutes the specimen and obscures the architecture the cytopathologist needs. This is the single most common technical error in thyroid FNA.
(C) Core needle biopsy has a genuine role in selected situations, including nodules that remain non-diagnostic after repeated fine needle sampling, and suspected lymphoma or anaplastic carcinoma where tissue architecture matters. None of those applies here. In a 6.6 mm subcapsular lesion an 18 gauge core needle also introduces a real risk of hematoma and of passing straight through the target.
(D) Needle track seeding after fine needle aspiration of the thyroid is vanishingly rare and is not a reason to modify technique. Peripheral-only sampling of a lesion this small is a reliable way to return another non-diagnostic or indeterminate result, which is the outcome you were trying to avoid.

Her result: atypia of undetermined significance with nuclear atypia. Indeterminate cytology on a subcentimeter nodule with no aggressive features and no nodal disease, so structured active surveillance is arranged, with a defined interval and an agreed trigger for intervention.

Keypoint: in thyroid aspiration the smaller needle and the lighter hand return more diagnostic material, not less.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. 2015 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.

steps.title: Step 3/6: Surveillance Ends
steps.scenario:
Four months later she returns for her scheduled surveillance scan.

    Initial     0.66 x 0.60 x 0.61 cm, ill-defined margin
    Now         0.76 x 0.64 x 0.87 cm, ill-defined margin

The maximum dimension has increased by 2.1 mm, which is below the 3 mm threshold conventionally used to define progression, though the volume has clearly increased. You repeat the aspirate: suspicious for malignancy, papillary thyroid carcinoma cannot be excluded.

On review of the images, the lesion abuts the anterior capsule of the right lobe.
steps.media: Load image: Side-by-side surveillance ultrasound, initial and four-month study, matched plane and scale. Caption: 'Initial and follow-up.'
steps.question: Which finding most strongly ends active surveillance for this patient?

options.text: (A) The upgrade in cytology from indeterminate to suspicious for malignancy
(B) The 2.1 mm increase in maximum dimension
(C) The persistently ill-defined margin, unchanged across both studies
(D) The subcapsular position of the lesion

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

A cytological upgrade is a change in what the lesion is, not merely in how big it is, and it is the finding that most clearly ends a surveillance strategy. Suspicious for malignancy carries a substantially higher risk of carcinoma than atypia of undetermined significance, and a nodule that climbs the Bethesda categories under observation has answered the question surveillance was asked to answer.

Why the others fail:
(B) Real growth, and deliberately just short of the conventional threshold. Had this been the only change it would have been a reason to shorten the interval rather than to operate, so a learner who picks it is applying the right rule to the weaker signal. Note also that the volume has increased more than the maximum dimension suggests, which is an argument for measuring in three planes rather than one.
(C) Unchanged findings do not end surveillance. The margin was ill-defined at the outset and was part of why she was watched closely rather than discharged. It is a baseline characteristic, not a progression event.
(D) Genuinely relevant and genuinely secondary. A lesion abutting the capsule has less parenchyma between it and the extrathyroidal tissues, which weakens the case for long-term observation, and it belongs in the conversation with the patient. On its own, without growth and without a cytological change, it would not have ended surveillance.

Keypoint: surveillance ends when the lesion changes category, not when it changes millimeters, and the two do not always move together.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. 2025 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985. Ali SZ, Baloch ZW, Cochand-Priollet B, et al. The 2023 Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology. Thyroid. 2023;33(9):1039-1044.

steps.title: Step 4/6: Before the Knife
steps.scenario:
Staging computed tomography shows a lesion confined to the right lobe with no abnormal nodes. Clinical stage is T1a N0.

She has no voice complaint, no prior neck surgery, and speaks normally in clinic. You plan a right thyroidectomy with isthmusectomy, using intraoperative nerve monitoring.
steps.question: What is your remaining obligation before surgery?

options.text: (A) Document vocal fold mobility, and consent explicitly for recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and for hypoparathyroidism
(B) Nothing further; nerve monitoring will identify the nerve, and a normal voice makes laryngoscopy unnecessary
(C) Send a baseline thyroglobulin to serve as the reference value for postoperative surveillance
(D) Obtain a baseline calcium and parathyroid hormone, since hypoparathyroidism is the commonest complication

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

A normal voice does not mean two normal vocal folds. Unilateral immobility can be compensated and clinically silent, and if it is discovered after the operation rather than before it, nobody can say whether the surgery caused it. This is the assessment that protects the patient and the surgeon at the same time, and it is an otolaryngology responsibility that belongs to nobody else on the team.

Why the others fail:
(B) Nerve monitoring is an adjunct for identification during the case and for prognostic information at the end of it. It is not a substitute for knowing the preoperative state of the folds, and it cannot retrospectively establish what the fold was doing the day before surgery.
(C) A preoperative thyroglobulin in an intact gland has no surveillance value. After a lobectomy the remaining lobe continues to produce thyroglobulin, which is why serial monitoring is not recommended in this setting at all. Ultrasound is the follow-up.
(D) Hypoparathyroidism is a real risk and belongs in the consent, but it is far less likely after a unilateral procedure than after a total thyroidectomy, and a baseline panel does not change the operative plan.

Keypoint: document the fold before you operate, because afterwards the question can no longer be answered.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020, section on preoperative and postoperative voice assessment.

steps.title: Step 5/6: Does Negative Mean Better?
steps.scenario:
The operation is uncomplicated. Final pathology:

    Papillary microcarcinoma, classical subtype, well differentiated
    Greatest dimension 0.45 cm, pT1a
    Extrathyroidal extension: not identified
    Vascular invasion: not identified
    Multicentricity: not identified
    Surgical margin: very close, less than 0.1 mm
    Non-neoplastic thyroid: lymphocytic thyroiditis with fibrosis and calcification
    BRAF V600E immunostain: negative

She has read the report before her follow-up appointment. She points at the last line and asks: "It says BRAF negative. Does that mean my prognosis is better?"
steps.media: Load image: Final pathology report, all patient and institutional identifiers redacted. Caption: 'Final histology.'
steps.question: How do you answer her?

options.text: (A) Her outlook is excellent, but that comes from the size, the absence of extrathyroidal extension and vascular invasion, and the clear nodes; BRAF status is not what determines it
(B) Yes; BRAF-negative tumors carry a lower recurrence risk, so her outlook is better than it would otherwise have been
(C) No; BRAF-negative papillary carcinomas tend to behave more aggressively and warrant closer surveillance
(D) Yes, and it also means she will not need radioiodine

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Answer the question she is really asking, which is whether she is going to be all right, and then attribute the answer to the right variable. Her outlook is excellent, and it is excellent because the tumor is 4.5 mm, confined to the gland, without vascular invasion or multifocality, with clear nodes. Those are the features that drive her risk. BRAF status is a detail on the same page, not the reason.

This matters more than it sounds. If you tell her the good news comes from the BRAF line, you have tied her reassurance to a weak variable, and if anything ever does go wrong she will remember that you told her a molecular result made her safe.

Why the others fail:
(B) Overstates a real but small effect. BRAF-positive tumors are associated with extrathyroidal extension, nodal disease, and recurrence in large series, but the effect size is modest, it is confounded by histological subtype, and it does not reclassify a pT1a tumor. The direction is mildly in her favor; the magnitude does not carry the sentence.
(C) Inverts the association. If anything, positivity is the adverse marker, and it becomes clinically meaningful mainly alongside a TERT promoter mutation, where the combination behaves considerably worse than either alone.
(D) Reaches the right conclusion by the wrong route. She does not need radioiodine, and the reason is that she has a pT1a tumor completely excised by lobectomy, not that a stain came back negative. Explaining a correct decision with a wrong mechanism leaves her unable to understand the next decision you make.

What BRAF is actually for, if she asks further, is three separate things, and most confusion comes from not saying which one is in play. It is diagnostic before surgery, where a positive result on indeterminate cytology effectively settles the diagnosis, because the mutation occurs essentially only in papillary carcinoma and its anaplastic derivatives. It is weakly prognostic, as above. And it is predictive of treatment eligibility, since BRAF and MEK inhibition is used in BRAF V600E anaplastic carcinoma and in radioiodine-refractory disease. Because she is negative, that last door is closed, and other drivers such as RET fusions would be the ones worth looking for in the future she will almost certainly never need.

On the margin she may also ask about: a clearance of less than 0.1 mm looks alarming on the page and is close to expected in a microcarcinoma, where the lesion sits near the capsule almost by definition. In a pT1a tumor with no extrathyroidal extension, no vascular invasion, and no multicentricity, it does not by itself call for further surgery.

Keypoint: give her the reassurance she deserves, and attach it to the findings that actually earned it.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. 2015 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020, section on molecular markers. Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. 2025 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985.

steps.title: Step 6/6: What Happens Now
steps.scenario:
She is discharged on the third postoperative day with the drain out and the wound clean. Final stage is pT1a pN0, a 4.5 mm classical papillary microcarcinoma, no extrathyroidal extension, no vascular invasion, no multicentricity. The left lobe is intact.

At her first clinic visit she asks two questions: whether she needs to take a tablet for the rest of her life, and how you will know if the cancer comes back.
steps.question: What is the follow-up plan?

options.text: (A) Periodic neck ultrasound, TSH checked periodically with levothyroxine started only if she becomes hypothyroid, and no serial thyroglobulin
(B) Serial thyroglobulin every six months as the primary surveillance test, since a rising level would signal recurrence
(C) Levothyroxine started now and titrated to suppress TSH below 0.1 microIU/mL, to reduce the risk of recurrence
(D) Completion thyroidectomy, because the surgical margin was less than 0.1 mm

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

After a lobectomy the surveillance test is ultrasound. You are looking at the thyroid bed, the remaining lobe, and the nodal compartments, and for a low-risk tumor of this size the interval is measured in years rather than months. Thyroid function is checked for her sake, not for the cancer's: roughly one in four to one in three patients becomes hypothyroid after a lobectomy and needs replacement, and the rest do not. So the honest answer to her first question is that she may need a tablet, that you will find out from a blood test rather than from a guess, and that many patients in her position never take one.

Why the others fail:
(B) The commonest misunderstanding after a lobectomy, and it comes from applying total-thyroidectomy logic to a patient who still has half a thyroid. The remaining lobe produces thyroglobulin, so the level reflects how much normal tissue she has rather than whether tumor has returned. Serial monitoring is not recommended in this setting, and a rise would generate anxiety and imaging without meaning anything.
(C) TSH suppression is not indicated for low-risk disease after lobectomy. The aim is a TSH in the normal range, low-normal if anything, and driving it below 0.1 buys her no reduction in recurrence risk while exposing her to the bone and cardiac costs of long-term thyrotoxicosis. She is 41 and will live with this for decades.
(D) The close margin is real and it looks alarming on the report, but it is close to expected in a microcarcinoma, where the lesion sits near the capsule almost by definition. In a pT1a tumor with no extrathyroidal extension, no vascular invasion, and no multicentricity, it does not by itself justify taking the other lobe. Choosing it converts a patient who may need no medication at all into one who certainly needs it for life.

One thing to add to the plan that is specifically yours: if her voice changes at any point after this operation, she needs her vocal folds looked at, and you documented them before surgery precisely so that the comparison is available.

Keypoint: after a lobectomy the surveillance test is the ultrasound, and the thyroid function test is for her symptoms rather than for her cancer.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. 2025 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985. Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.
